note: Refreshed every week by the program's research task. Each item says what changed, why it matters to a data engineer or architect, and how to test the claim yourself.

items.title: BigQuery: project and organisation settings can stop queries leaving a reservation for on-demand billing (GA)
items.summary: On 23 November 2026 BigQuery made two settings generally available: reservation_override_mode and disable_on_demand_billing. They are set per region with ALTER PROJECT SET OPTIONS or ALTER ORGANIZATION SET OPTIONS and decide whether a query may override its reservation and run on on-demand pricing, or must stay on the reserved slots.
items.why: Capacity commitments only cap the bill if nobody can step around them. This is a guardrail set once by the platform team instead of a rule in a wiki, and it is the concrete answer to an interviewer asking how you stop one team bypassing the reservation.
items.try: In module 7's cost section, take the Athena-style bytes-scanned exercise and write down which control would have stopped the expensive query: a budget alert, a per-query limit or a rule that forbids on-demand. Say which of the three acts before the money is spent.

items.title: Snowflake: more than one tag-based row access policy on the same table (preview)
items.summary: On 23 November 2026 Snowflake released, in preview, the ability for several tag-based row access policies to apply to one table or view. They combine with AND by default; setting a policy on the tag as PERMISSIVE combines it with OR. The release note lists no limits or edition requirements.
items.why: Row rules usually come from different owners: region from legal, business unit from finance. Layering independent policies through tags avoids one large policy that every team has to edit, but AND versus OR is now a design decision that can silently hide or expose rows.
items.try: In Org 3's access exercise, write two row rules (region and business unit) and work out by hand which rows a user sees when they combine with AND and when they combine with OR. Note which mistake leaks data and which only hides it.

items.title: Databricks: a system table with daily storage metrics for every managed table (GA)
items.summary: On 25 November 2026 Databricks made system.storage.table_metrics_history generally available. It holds one row per Unity Catalog managed table, materialized view and streaming table per daily cycle, with active, vacuumable and time-travel bytes and file counts, kept for 13 months. Databricks pays for the collection compute; foreign and Hive metastore tables are not covered.
items.why: Storage showback and finding tables that need VACUUM used to mean a custom crawler over table history. A system table turns both into a SQL query, and vacuumable bytes per table is exactly the number a cost review asks for.
items.try: In module 8's Delta lab, run optimize and vacuum on the table and record active files and removable files before and after. That is the per-table number this system table gives you every day for a whole catalog.

items.title: AWS WAF finds and protects LLM, MCP and agent-to-agent endpoints (GA)
items.summary: On 23 November 2026 AWS announced that the API Gateway API Portal discovers LLM, MCP and A2A endpoints behind API Gateway, load balancers and CloudFront across an organisation from traffic logs and configuration, flagging undocumented public MCP servers. A new WAF AI Security managed rule group checks protocol compliance, blocks malformed MCP and A2A messages and can call Bedrock Guardrails for prompt injection and sensitive data. The rule group is in 7 regions; WAF and Bedrock charges apply.
items.why: It adds a network layer to guardrails in layers: a check that runs before the request reaches your application, and an inventory of MCP servers nobody registered. It does not replace access checks on tools or output checks in the application.
items.try: In AI 6's guardrails exercises, list each layer (input, access, action, output, audit) and mark which ones a network rule in front of the endpoint could cover and which it cannot see at all.

items.title: Amazon OpenSearch Service supports OpenSearch 3.9: smaller vectors and an LLM judge for search relevance
items.summary: On 23 November 2026 Amazon OpenSearch Service added OpenSearch 3.9. For vectors it brings a half-float type with a 16-bit encoder, 2-bit and 4-bit scalar quantization and Base64 vector ingestion. The Search Relevance Workbench gains LLM-as-a-judge scoring through model connectors, reusing earlier judgments.
items.why: Vector memory is the first sizing question in a RAG design: 16 bits per dimension halves a float32 index, and 2-bit or 4-bit quantization cuts it much further at some cost in recall. A built-in judge makes it cheaper to measure that cost instead of guessing.
items.try: In AI 5's lens, redo the sizing of 10 million documents with 32, 16, 4 and 2 bits per dimension, then say how you would measure the recall you gave up before choosing.

items.title: Anthropic: Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (beta) keeps sealed safety copies in the customer's own bucket
items.summary: On 23 November 2026 Anthropic launched Enterprise Frontier Safeguards in beta. Eligible organisations get zero data retention, with encrypted copies of prompts and responses written to an S3 or Cloud Storage bucket in the customer's account. It applies to every request in a workspace, the customer reviews safety cases instead of Anthropic, and a customer-managed key is optional but permanent once attached.
items.why: It is a new retention pattern for regulated LLM workloads: the provider keeps nothing, and the evidence sits in storage you own and must operate. Several choices cannot be undone, which is the kind of trade-off a design answer should name before turning it on.
items.try: In AI 6's audit and governance section, write the three questions you would ask before enabling it: who can read the bucket, what happens when a write to it fails, and what you can no longer change afterwards.

items.title: Anthropic: Claude Managed Agents add scheduled runs, session budgets and a self-hosted option (beta)
items.summary: Managed Agents is Anthropic's hosted harness: a sandbox, sessions, memory stores and vaults around the model. Between June and November 2026 it gained scheduled deployments (9 June), session budgets (7 August), a server-checked automatic permission policy (10 September) and a fully self-hosted option on request (12 November). It is still a beta. On the model side, Claude Fable 5.2, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 all have a 1M-token context and set reasoning by an effort level.
items.why: The loop, the sandbox and the schedule are now things you can buy. What stays yours is the set of tools for your data, the permission rules, the budget per run and the check that says the work is done. Ask of any hosted harness what you ask of any managed service: what state lives there, how you export it, and what happens to running work in an outage.
items.try: Do exercise 4 of module AI 7 (a loop with four stop rules), then write down which of its four stop rules a session budget replaces and which you would still have to build.

items.title: OpenAI: the Agents API (public beta) is the new managed harness; the Assistants API ended and hosted Evals closes on 30 November
items.summary: OpenAI's Agents API, in public beta since 10 September 2026, runs a managed harness with durable sessions on OpenAI's sandbox or your own, and later added computer use, scheduled automations and background compaction by default. The Assistants API was shut down on 26 August 2026, and Agent Builder, the hosted Evals product and reusable prompts end on 30 November 2026. Prompt caching can now last 12 hours, with cache writes priced above normal input.
items.why: Two hosted agent products retired in one year is the lesson: keep prompts, tool definitions, eval sets and traces in your own repository and storage, behind an interface you own. A design that depends on a vendor's eval product has no regression gate the day it closes.
items.try: List every hosted feature one of your AI designs depends on and mark each as generally available, beta or preview. For each beta, write the one-line plan if it changes shape.

items.title: Google: Gemini 4 models, the Interactions API as the main API, and tool retrieval that loads tool definitions on demand (preview)
items.summary: Google released the Gemini 4 family (Argon, Carbon, Hydrogen and Neon) in October and November 2026, with a 1M-token context and thinking levels. The Interactions API, with background runs and stored state, is now the primary API for models and agents. Tool retrieval, in preview since 19 November, loads tool definitions only when a request needs them, including tools from remote MCP servers. Computer use became generally available on 30 October.
items.why: Tool definitions are context: forty tools can be a third of every prompt, paid for on every turn. Loading them on demand is the select move of context engineering done by the platform. Stored state on the provider's side raises a governance question: what is kept, for how long, and who may read it.
items.try: Do exercise 2 of module AI 7 (pack a context budget) with your own numbers: count the tokens of the tool definitions in one agent you use and work out their share of a 30-turn run.

items.title: xAI: Grok 4.7 prices cached input at a quarter of normal input; Grok Bot runs persistent agents with scheduled routines
items.summary: Grok 4.7, the current xAI API model since September 2026, has a 500k-token context and lists three prices: input, cached input at a quarter of that, and output. xAI's documentation describes Grok Bot as persistent agents on a cloud computer with connectors, MCP servers, scheduled routines and approval before sending, and Grok Build as a terminal coding agent with sub-agents, hooks and MCP. xAI has no published agent SDK or tracing tooling of its own.
items.why: Every large lab now prices cached input separately, so prompt order is a cost decision: a stable prefix is billed at a fraction, and one timestamp near the top loses it. Approval before sending is the ask rule of a harness, shipped as a product default.
items.try: Do exercise 1 of module AI 7 (order a prompt for caching), then price one of your prompts three ways: no cache, a cached stable prefix, and a prefix broken by a timestamp.

items.title: Databricks: a native Lakebase Postgres sink for Spark Structured Streaming is generally available
items.summary: On 23 November 2026 Databricks announced general availability of a built-in sink that writes Structured Streaming output straight into Lakebase (its managed Postgres) with one writeStream call, on Databricks Runtime 18 LTS and above. It handles batching, retries, connection reuse and upserts on a declared key, in micro-batch and Real-Time Mode; on serverless only the AvailableNow trigger runs. Writing to an outside PostgreSQL through a Unity Catalog connection is still in public preview.
items.why: The usual way to feed a serving database from a stream is a hand-written foreachBatch writer, which is where duplicate rows after a retry come from. A sink that upserts by key moves that risk into the platform, but the questions stay yours: what the key is, what happens to late and out-of-order rows, and how much write load Postgres can take.
items.try: In module 5's streaming lab, rerun the exactly-once-after-a-crash exercise and write down which key makes the sink's write idempotent; then say what would go wrong with an append-only sink after the same crash.

items.title: Snowflake: new dynamic tables with the default refresh mode now resolve to ADAPTIVE
items.summary: From 20 November 2026, a dynamic table created with the default REFRESH_MODE = AUTO resolves to ADAPTIVE when its query supports incremental refresh, and to FULL otherwise; before, it resolved to INCREMENTAL. Existing tables keep the mode they already have. To keep plain incremental refresh, without adaptive reinitialization, set REFRESH_MODE = INCREMENTAL yourself.
items.why: A changed default is a behaviour change nobody wrote in a pull request: two tables with the same SQL, created a week apart, can now refresh differently and cost differently. State the refresh mode in code, and check what a table actually resolved to before you promise a freshness or a credit number.
items.try: In 8.4, list which of your module 4 models you would make dynamic tables, and for each write the refresh mode you would set explicitly and why; then find the one whose query could not refresh incrementally.

items.title: Snowflake: COPY INTO and Snowpipe enforce CHECK constraints and log rejected rows (GA)
items.summary: Generally available since 19 November 2026: COPY INTO and Snowpipe now enforce a table's CHECK constraints and reject rows that break them. With error logging turned on for the table (ALTER TABLE ... SET ERROR_LOGGING = TRUE) and ON_ERROR = CONTINUE, rejected CSV, JSON and Parquet rows go to the table's error table with the error and usually the source record, so they can be fixed and reloaded in SQL. Tables without CHECK constraints or error logging behave as before.
items.why: This is a dead-letter queue and a contract check at the loading step, built into the warehouse. It catches bad rows before they reach a model, but only the rules you can write as a row-level CHECK: volume drops, late files and duplicates still need the tests from 9.2 and the write, audit, publish step.
items.try: Take the contract you wrote in 9.3 and mark each rule as either a row-level CHECK the loader could enforce or a table-level test it cannot; in module 5's lab, compare with what your dead-letter queue keeps for each bad record.

items.title: BigQuery Storage API v1beta1 is deprecated; Spark, Beam and Trino connectors need the v1 API
items.summary: On 25 November 2026 Google deprecated the BigQuery Storage API v1beta1. Since 20 November it is restricted to projects that used it between 1 March and 31 August 2026, and it shuts down fully on 31 August 2027, after which calls fail with NOT_FOUND. The release note says to move to the backward-compatible v1 API and to update connectors, naming the Spark BigQuery connector, the Apache Beam connector, the Trino plugin and the Simba JDBC and ODBC drivers.
items.why: Most teams never call this API by name: an old connector jar pinned in a Spark job does. Deprecations like this are found by an inventory of connector versions, not by reading code, and the nine-month window is the time to schedule the upgrade instead of meeting it during an incident.
items.try: For the batch path you built in module 7, list every connector and driver with its pinned version and who owns the upgrade; in 7.8, add the BigQuery read path to your map of the same design on Google Cloud.

items.title: Databricks: impact analysis in Unity Catalog lineage (beta)
items.summary: Since 23 November 2026, Unity Catalog lineage can show the downstream assets that depend on a table or a column, each with an impact level and its owner (beta). Genie Code can summarize the result and export the owners to a CSV file.
items.why: Before you drop or rename a column, the question is who breaks and who to tell. Lineage that answers with owners turns a schema change from a guess into a list of people; it is only as complete as the lineage captured, so jobs that read files directly or run outside the platform will be missing.
items.try: In O3's lab, run the lineage exercise for one column you would rename and write the notice you would send to each downstream owner; then name one consumer that column-level lineage would not see.

items.title: Claude Opus 4.5 is deprecated; API retirement on 22 January 2027
items.summary: On 23 November 2026 Anthropic deprecated Claude Opus 4.5 (claude-opus-4-5-20251101 and the claude-opus-4-5 alias), with retirement from the Claude API set for 22 January 2027; the notes recommend moving to Claude Opus 5.5. The same notes launch Enterprise Frontier Safeguards in beta: zero data retention for eligible organizations on the most capable models, with encrypted copies kept in a bucket in the customer's own cloud account.
items.why: A model id in a pipeline is a dependency with an end date. A gateway that maps a route name to a model, plus a golden-set eval gate, makes a retirement a config change you can test; a model id written into twenty jobs makes it a migration project with a deadline someone else chose.
items.try: In A6's lab, change the model behind one gateway route and rerun the regression gate exercise; note which golden-set cases you would add before trusting a new model on your own prompts.
